title: Nearby Galaxy Centaurus A
caption: The galaxy Centaurus A (NGC 5128), imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: Centaurus A, NG 5128 · constellation Centaurus · about 10 million light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: NASA Hubble image release (STScI). No published audience rating.

story: A dark lane of dust girdles the galaxy Centaurus A, also called NGC 5128, with blue clusters of newborn stars and dark dust filaments set among glowing orange gas. About 10 million light-years away in the constellation Centaurus, it hosts the active galactic nucleus nearest to Earth, and it has long been seen as an elliptical galaxy thrown into disarray by a recent collision with a smaller spiral.

It is the closest known case of one galaxy devouring another. A massive black hole, suspected to lie hidden at the center, is feeding on the smaller galaxy and may contain the mass of perhaps a billion stars packed into a region not much larger than our solar system. Infrared observations with another Hubble instrument looked through the dust to a twisted disc of hot gas around it, tilted differently from the black hole's axis.
Collisions like this were common in the early universe but are rare today, so having one this close gives astronomers a valuable laboratory for studying how galaxy mergers feed giant black holes.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Planetary Camera 2 took this visible-light image. The color mapping is not published.
understand.eye: This is a visible-light view, and the dust lane hides the core, which astronomers needed Hubble's infrared camera to see through.

behind.people: See full credit: E.J. Schreier (STScI), and NASA
behind.exposure: Observation dates per NASA: August 1, 1997 and January 10, 1998.
behind.technique: Not stated by the source (single frame, stack, mosaic or panorama unknown).

explore: Sir John Herschel was the first to report the object, in 1847, describing two halves of a nebula split by a broad dark band. In 1949 astronomers using a radio antenna in Australia identified Centaurus A as a powerful radio galaxy, and in 1954 Walter Baade and Rudolph Minkowski showed it to be a galaxy.
sources: NASA release: Hubble Provides Multiple Views of How to Feed a Black Hole
alt: A galaxy crossed by a dark dust lane, with blue star clusters and orange glowing gas.
